chapters.title: Chapter 5: From Paper Valuation to Real Money

lessons.title: Liquidation Preference and the Exit Waterfall

children.text: The news breaks: the startup you backed has been acquired for ₹60 crore. You own 1%. Is that ₹60 lakh for you? Almost certainly not. Between the headline price and your bank account sits the exit waterfall: a fixed order in which lenders, advisers, preference holders and finally equity holders are paid. This lesson builds a full waterfall step by step, shows how liquidation preferences change who gets what at different sale prices, and teaches you to read the clauses that decide it.

body.text: An exit waterfall pours money through the cap table in order. Debt and costs are paid first, then preference holders, and only then does the rest spread across equity. The lower the sale price, the more of it the top of the waterfall keeps.

children.text: The Building Blocks of a Liquidation Preference
A
liquidation preference
has four settings. Every term sheet chooses one option for each.

markDefs.definition: The right of a preference shareholder to receive a set amount, usually a multiple of what they invested, before equity holders in a sale, merger or winding up.

body.caption: The four settings of a liquidation preference

cells: Non-participating, participating, or participating with a cap
Senior (later rounds paid first) or pari passu (all series share equally)
Winding up only, or any "deemed liquidation event" such as a sale, merger or asset sale

body.latex: \text{Non-participating payout} = \max\left(\text{Preference},\ \text{As-converted share of what is left}\right)
body.caption: Take your money back or convert, whichever is higher

body.latex: \text{Participating payout} = \text{Preference} + \text{As-converted share of what is left}
body.caption: Take your money back and then share in the rest as well

children.text: Meet KisaanDrone

KisaanDrone Technologies Private Limited is a fictional Chandigarh startup offering drone crop spraying to farmers in Punjab and Haryana. Sanjay, a Mohali angel, holds 10,000 equity shares, 1% of the company. Here is the fully diluted cap table on an as-converted basis.
The Series A fund paid ₹20 crore for 25%, so the Series A post-money valuation was ₹80 crore. KisaanDrone also has ₹5 crore of venture debt, and any sale will cost ₹1 crore in banker and legal fees.
Building the Waterfall for a ₹60 Crore Sale

body.caption: Exit waterfall: KisaanDrone sold for ₹60 crore

cells: Repay venture debt and pay transaction costs
Series A (senior): preference of ₹20 crore vs converting to 25% of ₹54 crore = ₹13.50 crore. Takes the preference.
Seed (junior): preference of ₹4 crore vs converting and sharing ₹34 crore with equity, 10 ÷ 75 × ₹34 crore = ₹4.53 crore. Converts.
Remaining ₹34 crore shared by everyone holding converted or equity shares: 75% of the cap table

stats.label: Series A fund
stats.context: Its money back, 33% of the sale price for 25% ownership

body.text: A ₹60 crore sale is 25% below the ₹80 crore Series A valuation, and the Series A fund is completely protected. Everyone below it absorbs the shortfall. That is exactly what a liquidation preference is designed to do.

body.title: Run a simple waterfall
body.prompt: A startup with no debt is sold for ₹30 crore, with no transaction costs. Its only preference holder is a Series A fund that invested ₹12 crore for 30%, with a 1x non-participating preference. You hold 2% through equity shares. How much do you receive, in ₹ lakh? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Converting would give the fund 30% × ₹30 crore = ₹9 crore, less than its ₹12 crore preference, so it takes ₹12 crore. ₹18 crore remains for the other 70%. Your share = 2 ÷ 70 × ₹18 crore = ₹0.5143 crore, or ₹51.43 lakh, against a pro-rata ₹60 lakh.

children.text: The Same Cap Table at Five Sale Prices

body.caption: KisaanDrone payouts at different sale prices (1x non-participating, ₹ crore unless stated)

children.text: Three zones appear. At a very low price, the senior investor takes everything. In the middle, preferences are paid and equity holders share a shrinking remainder. Above a high enough price, every series converts, preferences stop mattering and everyone is paid in proportion to ownership. For KisaanDrone, the Series A fund converts once its 25% share of the net proceeds exceeds ₹20 crore, which means net proceeds above ₹80 crore.
Participating Preference: Double Dipping
Now suppose the Series A fund had negotiated a fully
participating preference
instead. It takes its ₹20 crore first and then also shares in the remainder as if converted.

markDefs.definition: A preference where the investor first takes its preference amount and then also shares in the remaining proceeds as if it had converted.

body.title: Sanjay's payout: Series A non-participating vs participating

body.caption: The ₹60 crore and ₹120 crore sales with a participating Series A (₹ crore unless stated)

children.text: With participation, the gap never closes. Even in a ₹300 crore sale, the Series A fund collects ₹88.5 crore instead of the ₹73.5 crore its 25% ownership alone would give it, ₹15 crore more, and every rupee comes out of the other holders. That is why participation is often capped, for example at 2x or 3x the investment, after which the investor is better off converting.

columns.label: Non-participating (1x)
points: Investor takes the higher of preference or as-converted share
Disappears in strong exits, when the investor converts
Fair to founders and angels in good outcomes
The balanced norm in most Indian venture rounds

columns.label: Participating (uncapped)
points: Investor takes the preference and then shares the rest
Never disappears, however large the exit
Transfers value from founders and angels in every outcome
A sign of weak negotiating power or a rescue round

body.title: Which term costs you most?
body.question: You hold equity shares. In a very large exit where every investor would happily convert, which Series A term reduces your payout the most?
options: 1x fully participating preference with no cap
Pari passu seniority with the seed round
body.explanation: In a very large exit, a non-participating investor converts and its preference disappears. A capped participating investor also ends up converting once its payout passes the cap. Only an uncapped participating preference keeps taking its preference on top of its full pro-rata share, no matter how large the exit.

children.text: Seniority: Who Stands First in the Preference Queue

When several series have preferences, seniority decides the order. Under a senior structure, the latest round is paid first, which is why KisaanDrone's Series A took all ₹14 crore in the ₹20 crore sale and the seed fund got nothing. Under
pari passu
, all series share the preference pool in proportion to their preference amounts.

markDefs.definition: Latin for "on equal footing": all preference series are paid at the same level, sharing any shortfall in proportion to their preference amounts.

body.label: KisaanDrone ₹20 crore sale, pari passu
body.context: The ₹14 crore available is split in the ratio of the ₹20 crore and ₹4 crore preferences, 20 : 4. The seed fund recovers something instead of nothing.

body.title: Equal footing
body.textWithBlank: When all preference series are paid at the same level, sharing any shortfall in proportion to their preference amounts, they are said to rank ___.
body.explanation: Pari passu means "on equal footing". The alternative is a senior structure, where later rounds are paid in full before earlier ones receive anything.

body.title: How this works legally in India, and what happens to ESOPs

children.text: Winding up.

Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and company law, preference shareholders already rank ahead of equity shareholders for return of capital. The multiple, participation and seniority details come from the company's Articles and the shareholders' agreement.
Sale of the company.

In a share sale, the buyer pays sellers for their shares, so the waterfall is usually implemented contractually: the shareholders' agreement and Articles require proceeds to be distributed according to the preference terms, often backed by drag-along rights.
Foreign investors.
FEMA pricing rules on transfers to and from non-residents can constrain how a contractual waterfall is implemented in practice.
ESOPs.

Vested options usually have to be exercised, paying the exercise price, or are cashed out net of it. Unvested options may lapse, or vest early under an acceleration clause. This example treated all ESOP holders as holding exercised shares for simplicity.
The exact mechanics depend heavily on drafting. Have a lawyer read the liquidation preference, deemed liquidation event and drag-along clauses together.

body.text: The waterfall includes more than share classes. Venture debt, unpaid vendor dues, employee dues, transaction costs, escrow holdbacks and founder or management carve-out bonuses can all come out before any shareholder is paid. Always ask what sits ahead of the preference stack, not just inside it.

body.title: The rescue term sheet
body.scenario: A struggling Jaipur travel startup, last valued at ₹150 crore, receives a ₹25 crore rescue offer. The new investor wants 2x participating preference with no cap, senior to all existing series. You hold 1.5% through equity shares, and existing CCPS investors already have ₹60 crore of 1x non-participating preference.
body.prompt: What would this term sheet do to your position, and what would you push for as an existing shareholder?
body.modelAnswer:
What it does:
1. The preference stack jumps. The new investor's 2x on ₹25 crore adds ₹50 crore, on top of the existing ₹60 crore, for ₹110 crore ahead of equity.
2. It is senior, so in any sale below about ₹110 crore after debt and costs, equity holders, including you, likely receive nothing.
3. It is participating with no cap, so even in a large exit the new investor takes ₹50 crore first and then its full pro-rata share of the rest.
4. Combined with the lower valuation typical of a rescue round, your 1.5% is diluted and pushed further down the waterfall.

What to push for:
1. 1x instead of 2x.
2. Non-participating, or at least participation capped at 2x to 3x.
3. Pari passu with existing series instead of strictly senior.
4. A management carve-out or incentive pool is common in rescues. Ask whether any value is reserved for existing common shareholders.
5. Pay-to-play for existing investors, so that those who do not support the rescue lose their own preferences, rather than every shareholder bearing the cost equally.

If the alternative is a shutdown, some version of these terms may still be better than nothing, but model the waterfall at several exit prices before you vote.

body.title: Reading a liquidation preference clause
steps: Find the multiple for each series: 1x, 1.5x, 2x or more.
Check whether each series is non-participating, participating or capped participating.
Confirm the seniority: senior by series or pari passu.
Read the definition of a liquidation or deemed liquidation event.
Add up the total preference stack and list any debt, dues or carve-outs ahead of it.
Model your payout at three to five sale prices, including one below the last round's post-money valuation.
Identify the sale price above which every series converts and preferences stop mattering.

cards.definition: The right to receive a set amount, usually a multiple of the investment, before equity holders in a sale or winding up.
The investor takes the higher of its preference or its as-converted share, not both.
The investor takes its preference and then also shares in the remainder as if converted.
A limit, such as 3x the investment, on total payout from a participating preference, above which the investor converts.
A preference paid in full before other series receive anything, usually held by later rounds.
All preference series paid at the same level, sharing any shortfall in proportion to their preference amounts.
A sale, merger or asset sale treated as a liquidation for the purpose of applying preferences.
The order in which sale proceeds are paid: debt and costs, preferences by seniority, then equity.

points: Sale proceeds flow in order: debt and costs, preferences by seniority, then everyone holding equity or converted shares.
A liquidation preference has four settings: multiple, participation, seniority and trigger.
Non-participating investors take the higher of their preference or as-converted share, so preferences disappear in large exits.
Participating preferences take the preference and a share of the rest, reducing equity payouts in every outcome.
Senior structures can wipe out earlier series in low sales. Pari passu shares the shortfall.
Model your payout at several sale prices, including below the last valuation, before you invest or vote on new terms.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or legal advice. KisaanDrone and the other companies and investors described are fictional, and the waterfall is simplified. Real distributions depend on detailed drafting, debt terms, ESOP treatment, tax and applicable law including FEMA. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a lawyer before investing.
